docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram shows the blocks of the Arm Motion Control board, how power and signals move between them, and how the board connects to the rest of the team.

  • Microcontroller: the board runs on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The Nano is powered from its own USB port and uses 3.3 V logic with a 0–3.3 V analog range.
  • Power: a 9 V DC wall adapter plugs into a barrel jack.
    • The input goes through a 1 A slow-blow fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode.
    • An LM317T, set by R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω, makes the 6.0 V motor rail.
    • An L7805 makes the 5 V logic rail.
    • Motor current never passes through the microcontroller board.
  • Actuator: an onsemi FAN8100N H-bridge drives a 6 V Pololu #2370 DC gearmotor. The motor has two wires, M+ and M−. RB0 and RB1 provide the two PWM inputs through PPS.
  • Debug:
    • A status LED on RE0.
    • A push button on RE1, using the weak pull-up.
    • Expansion header J4, which brings out 3.3 V, GND and the spare pins RA0, RA2, RB2 and RB3.
  • Team connection: the board connects to the Gripper & Object Handling board through the 8-pin ribbon cable.
    • It receives SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, OBJ_HELD and the analog SPEED_SET.
    • It sends GRIP_CMD and ARM_IN_POS.
    • Pin 7 (GRIP_FORCE) is not used on this board and is left open. Pin 8 is GND.
  • Ground: all grounds are tied together. This includes USB, the 9 V supply, the H-bridge and ribbon pin 8.

docs.title: H-Bridge Motor Driver
docs.text:
1. Pololu DRV8874 single brushed DC motor driver carrier

    • $11.94/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons PH/EN mode controls speed and direction with one PWM pin plus one GPIO, which matches our pin map. Most expensive of the three drivers. Integrated current sensing and regulation (IPROPI, VREF) limits motor current without an external shunt resistor. Needs PMODE and nSLEEP wired, which adds two connections compared with a two-input driver. Undervoltage, overcurrent and thermal protection, plus an nFAULT output the firmware can read. Includes 0.1" breakaway headers, so it can be hand soldered and tested on a breadboard.

  2. Adafruit DRV8871 DC motor driver breakout

    • $7.50/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Lower price Changing the current limit means swapping a resistor, not changing a reference voltage. Current limit set by a resistor, so the motor is protected without firmware. No current-sense output for the firmware to read Simple two-input interface and well documented by Adafruit.

  3. TB6612FNG Dual Motor Driver Carrier

    • $4.95/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Lowest price No current sensing or regulation. Two channels, so the second channel could be paralleled for 2 A continuous or kept as a spare. Three control inputs per channel plus a shared STBY pin, it uses more GPIO than our pin map 3 A peak current and PWM frequencies up to 100 kHz.

Choice: Option 1: Pololu DRV8874 single brushed DC motor driver carrier

Rationale: The PH/EN interface is the only one of the three that matches the pin map already shared with the team (one PWM pin and one direction pin), so no firmware or wiring changes are needed. Its 37 V range leaves a large margin on the 12 V rail, while the TB6612FNG is near its 13.5 V limit. Built-in current regulation matters here because the selected motor can draw a much higher stall current (about 5 A, extrapolated) than the carrier's continuous rating, so a driver that can limit current in hardware protects both the motor and the supply. The extra $4.44 over the DRV8871 buys these features.

docs.title: DC Motor
docs.text:
1. 34:1 Metal Gearmotor 25Dx67L mm HP 12V with 48 CPR Encoder

    • $56.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons 11 kg·cm stall torque at 300 rpm no-load speed gives the most torque margin Most expensive option Built-in two-channel Hall-effect quadrature encoder Stall current is 5.0 A, above the driver's continuous rating Datasheet and dimension drawing are available for the mechanical design Adds mass to the arm; the weight is not listed on the page and must be checked 4 mm D-shaft output. The encoder needs a 3.5 V to 20 V supply and its outputs swing from 0 V to Vcc

  2. Pololu 250:1 Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V

    • $23.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Very compact with metal gears, saves arm weight. Stall torque is only 1.6 kg·cm, about one seventh of Option 1 Low stall current fits any of the three drivers. Manufactor warns that stalling can damage the motor or gearbox The extended motor shaft allows a magnetic encoder to be added later. No encoder included Datasheet available

  3. Adafruit DC gearbox "TT" motor, 200 rpm, 3 to 6 VDC

    • $2.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Lowest price Stall torque is only 0.8 kg·cm at 6 V, too low for a loaded arm joint. Light with a 1:48 gearbox and 200 mm leads ending in 0.1" connectors. Rated 3 V to 6 V, needs a separate lower-voltage rail. TLow current (1.5 A stall at 6 V). No encoder included Choice: Option 2: Pololu 250:1 Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V

Rationale: The 6 V rail keeps the whole system on one motor rail as the power budget guidance recommends. Its stall torque is about fourteen times that of the TT motor, which gives margin while the real torque requirement of the arm is still unknown. The higher price is acceptable because the lower-cost motors would have to be replaced if the arm load turns out to be heavier.

docs.title: Position Sensor
docs.text:
1. Bourns 6639S-1-103, 10 kΩ single-turn conductive plastic precision potentiometer

    • $24.77/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Single analog output goes straight to RA0, using one pin and no driver code. Highest price of the three position sensors The reading is still valid after power loss, so no homing routine is needed. Mechanical contact wear over time. Not affected by the magnetic field of the motor. The wiper can be noisy, so the firmware should average several ADC samples. Used as a divider between 3.3 V and GND, the ±15% resistance tolerance does not matter because the reading is ratiometric.

  2. Bourns 3590S-2-103L, 10 kΩ 10-turn wirewound precision potentiometer

    • $17.78/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Lower price than Option 1 a joint that moves less than one revolution would use only a small part of the range, which wastes ADC resolution unless it is geared up. ±0.25% independent linearity, the best of the three. Wirewound elements change resistance in small steps rather than continuously. 2 W power rating and a −40 °C to +125 °C operating range. Larger body and a gear or pulley train would be needed, adding mechanical complexity

  3. Adafruit AS5600 magnetic angle sensor (STEMMA QT)

    • $5.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Lowest cost Needs a diametrically magnetized magnet centered on the shaft axis Contactless, so there is no wear The motor's magnets and currents can disturb the magnetic reading 12-bit absolute angle (4096 steps per revolution) Whether the analog OUT pin is available on this board must be confirmed Can be read over I2C or analog voltage. More design work needed

Choice: Option 1, Bourns 6639S-1-103. Rationale: The potentiometer matches the block diagram exactly: one analog wire to RA0 and nothing else to configure. A single-turn part fits an arm joint that moves less than one revolution, while the 10-turn Option 2 would waste most of its range. Unlike the AS5600, it is immune to the magnetic fields next to the motor, and it needs no magnet alignment. The extra cost ($6.99 more than Option 2) buys the correct travel range. If wear or cost becomes an issue, the AS5600 is the planned fallback.

docs.title: Motor Power Source
docs.text:
1. Mean Well GST60A12-P1J, 12 V 5 A desktop AC adapter

    • $19.40/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Regulated 12 V at 5 A with 120 mVp-p ripple, no extra voltage regulator is needed on the motor rail. The AC inlet is IEC C14, so a power cord must be purchased separately Overload and over voltage protection. At the motor's 5 A stall current the supply would be at 100% of its rating, no margin 2.1 × 5.5 mm barrel plug and 4,059 units in stock Tethered to a wall outlet, not portable Full datasheet is available

  2. Adafruit 12 V 5 A switching power supply

    • $24.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons 12 V at up to 5 A with a 2.1 mm barrel plug on about a 40 inch cable. The page listed it as out of stock when checked UL approved and RoHS compliant More expensive than Option 1 for the same rating Datasheet No clearly datasheet is provided on the product page

  3. Tenergy 12 V 2000 mAh NiMH battery pack (10S1P)

    • $36.49/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Portable, the arm can run without a wall outlet Maximum continuous discharge is 2 A, below the motor's stall current 12 V nominal at 2000 mAh (24 Wh) Voltage sags as the cells discharge and rises when fully charged Adjustable power supply Highest price No separate datasheet and a suitable charger must also be bought

Choice: Option 1, Mean Well GST60A12-P1J. Rationale: It is a regulated, safety-approved supply with a full datasheet and enough current for the motor, and it is in stock. Its price is lower than the Adafruit supply, which was out of stock and has no datasheet, and the battery cannot deliver the motor's peak current. This is a wall supply, not a USB power pack, as the assignment requires. The operating current will be checked against the 25% margin rule in the Power Budget page; the DRV8874 current limit keeps the motor below the supply's 5 A rating.

docs.title: Voltage regulation
docs.text: The 12V or 6V motor rail comes directly from the regulated Mean Well supply, so no additional regulator is needed for it. The Curiosity Nano is powered from USB and supplies the 3.3 V used by the potentiometer and logic. Power Budget details are to be calculated.

This page lists every component of the Arm Motion Control subsystem, taken from the subsystem schematic. It also lists the off-board items the system needs to run and the debugging and expansion hardware.

How the quantities were chosen:

  • One set for a breadboard prototype, one set for the subsystem PCB, and one or two spares, as the assignment asks.
  • Through-hole parts only (nothing smaller than 0805), so every part can be hand-soldered and used on a breadboard.
  • Parts that are in hand, handed out in class or kept in Peralta 109 (resistors, LEDs, fuses, IC sockets, headers) are still listed, but they are not on a purchase request.

The table is sorted by vendor, one section per purchase request. Prices and stock were checked on the vendor pages on 2026-10-30 and should be re-checked before the order is sent.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is the Arm Motion Control subsystem of Team 107 Simple Educational Robotic Arm. It is drawn in KiCad 9 with US/ANSI symbols, and parts are joined by wires rather than net labels wherever possible, so the signal path can be followed by eye. The sheet has five blocks:

  • Power: a 9 V DC barrel jack feeds a 1 A slow-blow fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity Schottky diode, giving VIN_PROT of about 8.55 V. VR1 is an LM317T set to 6.0 V by R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω, using Vout = 1.25 V × (1 + 910 / 240) = 6.0 V. This 6 V rail is the motor rail. VR2 makes the +5 V logic rail for the H-bridge VCC and the power LED DS1. Each regulator has 0.33 µF on its input and 0.1 µF on its output. Test points TP1 and TP2 are on the 6 V and 5 V rails.
  • Microcontroller: PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, powered from its own USB port with 3.3 V logic.
  • Motor drive: an onsemi FAN8100N H-bridge drives the 6 V Pololu #2370 gearmotor through M+ and M−. The motor has only these two pins. RB0 and RB1 supply PWM through PPS. The motor supply has 47 µF and 0.1 µF bulk and decoupling capacitors.
  • Debug and expansion:
    • A status LED on RE0.
    • A push button on RE1, using the weak pull-up.
    • J4, a 6-pin expansion header carrying 3.3 V, GND, RA0, RA2, RB2 and RB3.
  • Team ribbon: pins 1 to 8 carry, in order:
    • SAFE_OK (in)
    • RUN_REQ (in)
    • GRIP_CMD (out)
    • OBJ_HELD (in)
    • ARM_IN_POS (out)
    • SPEED_SET (analog in)
    • pin 7, which is not used on this board
    • GND

The three digital inputs have 10 kΩ pull-downs, so an unplugged cable reads 0, which means stop. The two outputs have 330 Ω series resistors. SPEED_SET has a 1 kΩ / 0.1 µF RC filter.

Figure 1: Arm Motion Control schematic

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This power budget checks that every supply and regulator on the Arm Motion Control board (schematic Rev C) can deliver the worst-case current its loads can draw, with a 25 % safety margin. The board has two independent sources, and their grounds are tied together on the board:

  • 9 V wall adapter (MEAN WELL GST25A09-P1J, 2.55 A) → J1 → F1 (1 A slow-blow) → D1 (1N5819), giving about 8.55 V. This feeds two regulators:
    • +6 V motor rail: VR1, an LM317T set by R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω. It feeds the FAN8100N output stage (PVCC) and the Pololu #2370 6 V gearmotor.
    • +5 V logic rail: VR2, an L7805CV. It feeds the FAN8100N logic (VCC) and the power LED DS1.
  • USB port of the PC (500 mA) → the Curiosity Nano's MIC5353 LDO → the +3.3 V rail for the PIC18F57Q43, the debug LED, the ribbon outputs and expansion header J4.

All major parts are listed with their absolute maximum current ratings from the datasheets. Each rail table uses the worst case a part can draw in this circuit. For example, the motor is counted at its 0.67 A stall current, and the LEDs at the current set by their resistors. Every number has its source in the last column of the spreadsheet.

Figure 1: Power budget, page 1. Major components, +6 V rail and +5 V rail (click to enlarge).

Figure 2: Power budget, page 2. +3.3 V rail, external sources, fuse and thermal checks (click to enlarge).

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The budget shows the following:

  • Every rail and source has headroom at worst case. The tightest point is the +6 V rail, where motor stall plus margin uses about 62 % of the LM317T's 1.5 A rating.
  • The fuse is sized correctly. Worst-case input current through F1 is about 947 mA, under the 1 A rating. F1 is slow-blow, so it rides through motor start-up and short stalls, but it still opens on a sustained fault. In normal running the motor draws about 0.1–0.2 A, far below this.
  • VR1 needs a heatsink. At worst case it dissipates (8.55 − 6) V × 0.93 A ≈ 2.4 W, which is too much for a bare TO-220. The Aavid 577102B00000G heatsink is in the BOM. VR2 dissipates only about 0.08 W and needs none.
  • The FAN8100N stays well inside its limits. Its 1.5 A per-channel output rating is more than twice the motor's stall current. Its estimated saturation loss at stall, about 0.6 W, is under the 2.0 W package rating.
  • The 9 V input gives the LM317T enough dropout margin. After the reverse-polarity diode the input is 8.55 V, and the LM317T needs about 6 V + 2 V = 8 V.
  • One small risk is the LM317T minimum load. The R11 / R12 divider draws 5.2 mA. That is above the typical 3.5 mA minimum load in the datasheet but below its 10 mA worst case. With the motor off, the 6 V rail could drift slightly high. If this shows up on the bench, a smaller divider (for example R11 = 120 Ω, R12 = 453 Ω) fixes it.

Two values are estimates rather than datasheet figures: the 25 mA allowance for the MCU core and the 100 mA allowance for the on-board debugger. Both are labeled as estimates in the spreadsheet.
